Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 90, verse 1–2:

Surat al-Balad is Meccan [Narrated by Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: Surat "La uqsimu bihadha al-balad" was revealed in Makkah. See: al-Durr al-Manthur: 8/516.]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

* *

﴿I swear by this city﴾, meaning: I swear by this city, meaning Makkah. ﴿And you are free [ḥill]﴾, that is, lawful, ﴿in this city﴾, you may do in it whatever you wish of killing and taking captives, and there is no sin upon you in that as there is upon people. Allah the Exalted made Makkah lawful for His Prophet ﷺ on the day of the Conquest, so that he fought and killed, and ordered the killing of Ibn Khatal, who was clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah [Narrated by al-Bukhari in Hajj, chapter on entering the Haram and Makkah without ihram: 4/58, and in Jihad, chapter on killing the captive and killing by patient restraint; and Muslim in Hajj, chapter on the permissibility of entering Makkah without ihram, no. (1357): 2/989–990.], and Miqyas ibn Subabah and others [Ibn Hajar attributed it in al-Kafi al-Shaf, p. 184, to Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i. See also Sirat Ibn Hisham: 4/52.]. So he made the blood of some people lawful and forbade the blood of others, and said: Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe [See: Sirat Ibn Hisham: 4/46.], then he said: Indeed Allah made Makkah sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth, and it was not lawful for anyone before me, nor is it lawful for anyone after me, and it was only made lawful for me for an hour of a day; it is forbidden by Allah's sanctity until the Day of Resurrection [A portion of a hadith narrated by al-Bukhari in Hajj, chapter on the virtue of the Haram: 3/449, and Muslim in Hajj, chapter on the sanctity of Makkah, its game, its grass and its trees, no. (1353): 2/986.].

The meaning is that when Allah the Exalted swore by Makkah, this indicated its great status together with its sanctity. So He promised His Prophet ﷺ that He would make it lawful for him so that he would fight in it, and that He would open it at his hand. This is a promise from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that He would make it lawful for him.

Shurahbil ibn Sa'd said: The meaning of His saying, "And you are free in this city," is: they consider it forbidden to kill game in it, yet they consider it lawful to expel you and kill you?

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 90, verses 3–6:**

﴿And the begetter and what he begot﴾, meaning Adam, peace be upon him, and his offspring.

﴿We have certainly created man in toil﴾. Al-Walibi related from Ibn 'Abbas: "in hardship." Al-Hasan said: "He endures the calamities of this world and the severities of the Hereafter." Qatadah said: "In hardship; you will never meet him except that he is struggling with the affairs of this world and the Hereafter."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: [in severity. 'Ata' said, from Ibn 'Abbas]: [[What is between the brackets is from "A".]] "In the severity of his creation: his carrying, his birth, his nursing, his weaning, his livelihood, his life, and his death."

'Amr ibn Dinar said: "At the time his teeth come out." Yaman said: "Allah has not created any creature that struggles as much as the son of Adam does, and yet he is the weakest of creatures." The root of *kabad* (toil) is hardship.

Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, 'Atiyyah and al-Dahhak said: it means "upright, of balanced stature," and every other creature walks bent over. This is also a report from Muqsim, from Ibn 'Abbas. [And the root] [[Omitted from "B".]] of *kabad* is "evenness and straightness."

Ibn Kaysan said: "Upright, his head in his mother's belly. When Allah permits him to come out, his head turns toward his mother's feet."

Muqatil said: "*In kabad*" means "in strength."

It was revealed concerning Abu al-Ashaddayn, whose name was Usayd ibn Kaldah al-Jumahi. He was strong and powerful; he would place an Ukazi hide under his feet and say: "Whoever can remove me from it will get such and such." No one could pull it from beneath his feet except by cutting it, and the place of his feet would remain.

﴿Does he think﴾, meaning Abu al-Ashaddayn, because of his strength, ﴿that no one has power over him﴾, meaning he thinks, because of his might, that Allah the Exalted has no power over him. It is also said that this refers to al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah.

﴿He says, "I have squandered wealth"﴾, meaning "I have spent," ﴿abundant wealth﴾, meaning much of it piled upon one another, from *talbid* (matting together), in enmity toward Muhammad (ﷺ). Abu Ja'far recited *lubbadan* with a shaddah on the *ba'*, as the plural of *lab*, like *raki'* and *ruka'*. The others recited it with the light form, as the plural of *libdah*, and it is also said it is a singular like *qutham* and *hutam*.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 90, verses 7–11:**

﴿Does he think that no one sees him?﴾ Sa'id ibn Jubayr said, [and Qatadah: "Does he suppose"] [[The words in the parentheses are missing from manuscript "A".]] that God does not see him, and that He will not ask him about his wealth: from where he earned it and where he spent it.

Al-Kalbi said: He was lying in his claim, "I spent such-and-such," when he had not spent everything he claimed. It means: "Does he suppose that God, Mighty and Majestic, did not see that from him, so that He would know the amount of his expenditure?" Then He reminded him of His blessings so that he would take heed, saying: ﴿Did We not make for him two eyes, and a tongue, and two lips?﴾ Qatadah said: The blessings of God are manifold, by which He makes you acknowledge Him so that you may give thanks. It has also come in a hadith that God, Mighty and Majestic, says: "Son of Adam, if your tongue disputes with you concerning what I have forbidden you, then I have helped you against it with two lids, so close them. If your sight strays toward some of what I have forbidden you, then I have helped you against it with two lids, so close them. If your private part strays toward what I have forbidden you, then I have helped you against it with two lids, so close them." [[See: Ibn Kathir: 4/513; al-Durr al-Manthur: 8/521.]]

﴿And We guided him to the two highways [al-najdayn].﴾ Most of the exegetes said: the path of good and evil, of truth and falsehood, of guidance and misguidance, like His saying: "Indeed, We guided him to the way; either he is grateful or he is ungrateful" (Qur'an 76:3). Muhammad ibn Ka'b reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning "and We guided him to the two highways" that he said: "The two breasts." This is also the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Dahhak. Al-najd is a path that rises upward.

﴿But he did not attempt the steep ascent [al-'aqabah].﴾ It means: Why did he not spend his wealth on that which would permit him to free necks (slaves) and feed the hungry in times of hunger, which would have been better for him than spending it on hostility toward Muhammad (ﷺ)? This is the view of Ibn Zayd and a group.

It was also said: "Fa-la-iqtahama al-'aqabah" means he did not storm it, nor did he cross it. Al-iqtiham (storming) means entering into a difficult matter. The mention of the "'aqabah" here is a parable that God struck for striving against the self, desire, and Satan in the works of righteousness. He made him like one who undertakes the climbing of a steep ascent. The meaning is: he did not impose upon himself the hardship of freeing a slave or feeding. This is the meaning of the statement of Qatadah.

It was also said: He likened the weight of sins upon their perpetrator to a steep ascent, so when he frees a slave and feeds, he is like one who has stormed the ascent and crossed it.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar that this 'aqabah is a mountain in Hell. [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 30/201. Al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (8/522) added its attribution to Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim.]]

al-Hasan and Qatadah said: It is a severe steep ascent in the Fire, short of the Bridge (al-jisr), and they storm it by obedience to God, the Exalted. [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 30/202. See also: al-Durr al-Manthur: 8/523.]]

Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and al-Kalbi said: It is a path (sirat) laid over Hell, like the edge of a sword, a journey of three thousand years, level, ascending and descending. On its two sides are hooks and grappling irons, like the thorns of the sa'dan plant. Some are saved intact, some are saved but torn, and some are thrown down headlong into the Fire. Among the people is one who crosses like a flashing lightning, and among them is one who crosses like a violent wind, and among them is one who crosses like a horseman, and among them is one who crosses like a man running, and among them is one who crosses like a man walking, and among them is one who crawls crawling, and among them are those who slip, and among them are those who are thrown into the Fire.

Ibn Zayd said: He means: "Why did he not take the path in which there is salvation?"

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 90, verses 7–11:**

﴿Does he think that no one sees him?﴾ Sa'id ibn Jubayr said, [and Qatadah: "Does he suppose"] [[The words in the parentheses are missing from manuscript "A".]] that God does not see him, and that He will not ask him about his wealth: from where he earned it and where he spent it.

Al-Kalbi said: He was lying in his claim, "I spent such-and-such," when he had not spent everything he claimed. It means: "Does he suppose that God, Mighty and Majestic, did not see that from him, so that He would know the amount of his expenditure?" Then He reminded him of His blessings so that he would take heed, saying: ﴿Did We not make for him two eyes, and a tongue, and two lips?﴾ Qatadah said: The blessings of God are manifold, by which He makes you acknowledge Him so that you may give thanks. It has also come in a hadith that God, Mighty and Majestic, says: "Son of Adam, if your tongue disputes with you concerning what I have forbidden you, then I have helped you against it with two lids, so close them. If your sight strays toward some of what I have forbidden you, then I have helped you against it with two lids, so close them. If your private part strays toward what I have forbidden you, then I have helped you against it with two lids, so close them." [[See: Ibn Kathir: 4/513; al-Durr al-Manthur: 8/521.]]

﴿And We guided him to the two highways [al-najdayn].﴾ Most of the exegetes said: the path of good and evil, of truth and falsehood, of guidance and misguidance, like His saying: "Indeed, We guided him to the way; either he is grateful or he is ungrateful" (Qur'an 76:3). Muhammad ibn Ka'b reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning "and We guided him to the two highways" that he said: "The two breasts." This is also the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Dahhak. Al-najd is a path that rises upward.

﴿But he did not attempt the steep ascent [al-'aqabah].﴾ It means: Why did he not spend his wealth on that which would permit him to free necks (slaves) and feed the hungry in times of hunger, which would have been better for him than spending it on hostility toward Muhammad (ﷺ)? This is the view of Ibn Zayd and a group.

It was also said: "Fa-la-iqtahama al-'aqabah" means he did not storm it, nor did he cross it. Al-iqtiham (storming) means entering into a difficult matter. The mention of the "'aqabah" here is a parable that God struck for striving against the self, desire, and Satan in the works of righteousness. He made him like one who undertakes the climbing of a steep ascent. The meaning is: he did not impose upon himself the hardship of freeing a slave or feeding. This is the meaning of the statement of Qatadah.

It was also said: He likened the weight of sins upon their perpetrator to a steep ascent, so when he frees a slave and feeds, he is like one who has stormed the ascent and crossed it.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar that this 'aqabah is a mountain in Hell. [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 30/201. Al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (8/522) added its attribution to Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim.]]

al-Hasan and Qatadah said: It is a severe steep ascent in the Fire, short of the Bridge (al-jisr), and they storm it by obedience to God, the Exalted. [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 30/202. See also: al-Durr al-Manthur: 8/523.]]

Abdul-Wahid al-Maliḥi informed us: Abu Mansur Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Sam'an informed us: Abu Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn 'Abd al-Jabbar al-Rayyani narrated to us: Humayd ibn Zanjawayh narrated to us: 'Abdullah ibn Salih narrated to us: al-Layth ibn Sa'd narrated to me: Ibn al-Hadi narrated to me, from 'Umar ibn 'Ali ibn Husayn, from Sa'id ibn Marjana, who said: I heard him narrating from Abu Hurayra, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever frees a believing neck, Allah will free for every limb of his a limb of his from the Fire, until He frees his private part for his private part." [Related by al-Bukhari in al-Ayman wal-Nudhur, chapter on the saying of Allah Most High: (or the freeing of a neck), 11/599; Muslim in al-'Itq, chapter on the virtue of emancipation, no. (1509): 2/1148; and the author in Sharh al-Sunna: 9/351-352.]

He said: "If you have shortened the sermon, you have broadened the request. Free the soul and release the neck." I said: "Are they not one and the same?" And the milch camel (al-manha al-wakuf), (i.e., one abundant in milk), and spend on the wrongdoing kinsman. If you cannot do that, then feed the hungry and give drink to the thirsty, command what is right and forbid what is wrong. If you cannot do that, then restrain your tongue except for good." (294); and the author in Sharh al-Sunna: 9/354. al-Haythami said in Majma' al-Zawa'id: 4/240: "Ahmad narrated it and its narrators are trustworthy."]

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 90, verse 15–20:

﴿An orphan near of kin﴾, i.e., having a relationship (qarabah), meaning an orphan who has a kinship tie between you and him.

﴿Or a needy person in misery﴾. He has clung to the dust because of his poverty and hardship. Mujahid said, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas: he is one thrown down in the dust with nothing to shield him. And "al-matrabah" is the verbal noun of taraba, yatrabu, taraban and matrabatan, meaning he became poor.

﴿Then he became one of those who believed﴾. This shows that such closeness to others benefits only together with faith. It is also said that "thumma" (then) here means "wa" (and). ﴿And they enjoined one another to patience﴾: some of them urged others to patience in obeying Allah's obligations and commands, ﴿and enjoined one another to compassion﴾: compassion toward people.

﴿Those are the companions of the right hand. But those who disbelieved in Our signs are the companions of the left hand. Over them will be a fire closed in (mu'sadah)﴾: its gates will be sealed shut upon them, so no relief enters it and no release comes out of it.

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and Hafs recited it with a hamzah here and in al-Humazah (ascha, "u'sadah" form with hamzah), while the others recited it without hamzah. Both are dialectal variants. It is said: "aṣadtu al-bab" and "awṣadtu al-bab" when one closes and locks the door. It is also said that the meaning of the hamzah form is "closed tightly," and the form without hamzah means "locked."

[[The Imam Abu Zur'ah Ibn Zanjalah said in his book "Hujjat al-Qira'at," p. (766): "Whoever recited it with hamzah made it (mu'selah / mu'sadah) from (aṣadtu al-bab), i.e., I closed it tightly, like amantu. The first radical of the verb is a hamzah; you say āṣada yu'ṣidu i'ṣādan. Whoever omitted the hamzah derived it from (awṣada yuṣidu iṣādan), where the first radical is a waw. Al-Kisa'i said: awṣadtu al-bab and aṣadtuhu when I bolted it."]]
